newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN CONSTITUTION TO PROTECT LOCAL SURCHARGES.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN CONSTITUTION TO PROTECT LOCAL SURCHARGES.

text.p: Constitutional negotiators have proposed that property rates and surcharges on service fees should be the major sources of income for municipalities under a new South African constitution to be implemented next year.

African National Congress negotiator Barbara Hogan and National Party counterpart Theo Alant reported tentative agreement on funding to a constitutional sub-committee trying to iron out flaws in a draft constitution adopted in May.

Hogan told Reuters afterwards that the two sides, who together have determined most of the major aspects of the draft constitution, had agreed in a private meeting to give constitutional protection to service fee surcharges.
She said the agreement was subject to ratification by their respective political parties and the Constitutional Assembly.
"We agreed that with the possibility of privatisation, it was necessary to ensure that municipalities do not lose service charge profits as a key revenue source," she said.

South Africa has committed itself to the full or partial privatisation of many state assets. The state-owned Eskom utility, which delivers electricity to most municipalities, is amongst likely targets for partial privatisation.
"Local governments' chief forms of revenue are through property taxes and...specifically the profits or the surplusses that they raise on water and electricity.
"We felt that that right needs to be more specifically stated within the fiscal powers of municipalities," Hogan said.
The ANC and the NP would propose that municipalities should be able to impose surcharges on electricity, water and other service charges even when the service was provided by an outside contractor.
Alant told the committee that other key provisions of the agreement between the NP and ANC included an assurance that no tax could be levied simultaneously by two levels of local government.
This would mean, for example, that a metropolitan council and a municipality within its area would not both be able to levy a property tax.

Alant said the two sides agreed that property taxes would be based on the market value of a property and would be levied at a rate decided by the local authority within parameters determined by national legislation.
